summary:
CoastLens is a web tool that watches the mangrove forests of Karachi’s coast, from Rehri Goth to Port Qasim, using NASA-ISRO’s NISAR radar satellite. A mangrove forest can look thick and green from above while it is thinning inside, and optical satellites only see the canopy. NISAR’s L-band radar works through cloud and at night, and its long wavelength reflects off trunks and branches, so a weaker echo can signal a weaker forest. It returns every twelve days.

Mangroves in our study area have grown overall since 1985, but in seven zones the forest kept shrinking. In one year of NISAR data we flagged eight patches where the echo faded, covering about 63 hectares out of roughly 18,000. That is where conservation teams should go first, instead of searching the whole forest by boat.

Radar shows where the signal changed, not why, so every alert is a question for a field visit, not a verdict. CoastLens is endorsed by Saltwater Marina and developed with Mangrove Crew. Because NISAR covers the whole world, the method can be applied to any mangrove coast.
details:
What it does: CoastLens monitors the mangrove forests of Karachi’s coast, from Rehri Goth to Port Qasim, and shows conservation teams where to send a field visit first. It maps where NISAR radar observations have changed and flags the patches that may be changing structurally.

How it works: NISAR’s L-band radar sends its own signal and works through cloud, haze and night, which matters on a coast where the monsoon hides the ground for weeks. Its long wavelength passes the leaves and reflects off trunks and branches, so a weaker echo can mean a weaker forest. We processed one year of NISAR observations (about every 12 days) and compared them with the long satellite record of mangrove extent. Across the whole area the forest signal held steady. Patch by patch, we found seven zones where the forest kept shrinking over the long record. In the past year, we flagged the eight largest patches where the echo faded, which random noise does not produce. They cover about 63 hectares out of roughly 18,000. On our interactive map, a user can click any flagged patch and see the evidence behind it.

Benefits: Teams no longer have to search the whole forest by boat. They can start with 63 hectares instead of 18,000, saving time and money. CoastLens is endorsed by Saltwater Marina, which works with the fishing community of Rehri Goth, and is developed with Mangrove Crew.

Limits: Radar shows where the echo changed, not why. Tide, rain and wet mud also move the signal. Every alert is a question for a field visit, not a verdict, and none has been verified on the ground yet. One year of data is not yet a trend.

Goal: Because NISAR covers the whole world, the same method can protect other mangrove coasts. Only the map area changes.

Tools: NISAR L-band data, Global Mangrove Watch, Landsat and Sentinel imagery, Python for data processing, and a JavaScript web app (Vercel) with interactive maps.
